summary: The talk traces the evolution of LLMs from scaling laws to the emerging frontier of reinforcement learning for autonomous coding. Beginning with the 2020 scaling laws breakthrough, Chowdhery explains the power law relationship between compute, data, parameters, and model performance, noting generalization across domains. She highlights emergent behaviors in large models, particularly chain-of-thought reasoning demonstrated in PaLM at 540B parameters, where asking models to show reasoning chains improved math performance and generalized across languages, puzzles, and multitask understanding. This reasoning capability enabled instruction-following, making chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini possible through RLHF, where human preference data trained models to prefer certain responses, with gains in both chat and code. As pre-training gains potentially plateau, Chowdhery pivots to inference-time scaling, which is cheap relative to training costs reaching tens of millions of dollars. Two approaches emerged: majority voting/self-consistency and sequential revision, showing predictable gains in verifiable domains like math and coding where unit tests and compilers serve as automated verifiers. However, inference-time scaling has significant limitations: correct generations can be very rare, requiring potentially 10,000 samples, making it impractical for real-world impact. Chowdhery argues RL can train models to generate correctly during training rather than relying on massive sampling at inference, referencing David Silver's 'era of experience' concept. She then details why scaling RL is even more challenging than scaling LLMs: the system stack requires keeping multiple copies of models (PPO needs four, GRPO reduces to three), managing both training and inference loops, and dealing with reward hacking when neural reward models are involved. Autonomous coding offers a solution because built-in verification—execution feedback, unit tests, SWE-bench verified scores—enables better reward function design. Chowdhery positions Reflection.ai's mission as building superintelligence starting with autonomous coding as the root node problem, with a team of about 35 pioneers. In Q&A, she notes that building coding agents requires multiple LLM calls and capabilities, with whether one or multiple models is used being a secret sauce. She distinguishes the 'era of experience' from simulation: in gaming, scenarios can be envisioned and rollouts are possible, but real-world applications have imperfect rollouts requiring actual experience and data collection.

sections.title: Introduction to LLMs and Scaling Laws
sections.summary: Chowdhery introduces her background at Google on PaLM and Gemini, now working on autonomous coding with RL. She recaps the 2020 scaling laws breakthrough showing power law relationships between compute/data/parameters and model performance, with generalization across domains. As models got bigger, benchmarks improved toward saturation.

sections.title: Emergent Behavior in LLMs
sections.summary: Discusses emergent capabilities in large models, particularly chain-of-thought reasoning demonstrated in PaLM. Shows that asking models to output reasoning chains improved math problem solve rates, with performance increasing with model size (up to 540B parameters). This generalized across languages, puzzles, and multitask understanding, leading to various prompting techniques like step-by-step reasoning.

sections.title: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)
sections.summary: Explains how reasoning capabilities enabled instruction-following, making chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini possible. RLHF uses human preference data to train models to prefer certain responses, showing gains in both chatbot and code applications. Raises the question of whether pre-training is hitting a performance wall.

sections.title: Inference-Time Scaling and Verification
sections.summary: Introduces inference-time scaling as a cheaper alternative to costly training. Two approaches: majority voting/self-consistency (generating multiple responses and voting) and sequential revision (iteratively improving responses). Shows predictable gains in verifiable domains like math and coding, where unit tests and compilers serve as verifiers. Stanford colleague's work demonstrates DeepSeek model achieving high HumanEval scores with more samples.

sections.title: Challenges with Inference-Time Scaling
sections.summary: Explains limitations of inference-time scaling: correct generations can be very rare, requiring potentially 10,000 samples to find correct solutions, making it impractical for real-world impact. Majority voting works in verifiable domains but doesn't solve the problem of generating correct answers consistently during training.

sections.title: The Next Frontier: Reinforcement Learning for Correct Generation
sections.summary: Argues that RL is the next frontier for scaling, referencing David Silver's 'era of experience' concept—progressing from simulation (AlphaGo/AlphaZero) through human data scaling to experience-based RL. Shows o1 results demonstrating test-time compute improvements in math with RL. Positions coding as a prime domain for RL due to automated verification capabilities.

sections.title: Challenges in Scaling RL
sections.summary: Details why scaling RL is more challenging than scaling LLMs. The system stack requires managing multiple model copies: PPO needs four copies (reference, reward, value, policy) arranged across GPUs, while DeepSeek's GRPO eliminates the value model reducing to three. RL combines both a training loop and inference loop. On the ML side, reward hacking is a significant problem when neural reward models judge correctness. Autonomous coding mitigates this because execution feedback and unit tests enable better reward function design, as seen in SWE-bench verified scores.

sections.title: Autonomous Coding as a Prime Domain for RL
sections.summary: Explains that autonomous coding is a great domain for scaling RL due to verification capabilities—execution feedback and unit tests allow designing better reward functions. However, real-world impact requires generalizing beyond code generation to end-to-end software engineering workflows with many more parts to the system.

sections.title: Reflection.ai's Mission
sections.summary: Describes Reflection.ai's mission to build superintelligence starting with autonomous coding as the root node problem. The team has about 35 pioneers with backgrounds in LLMs and RL. Q&A covers whether one generalist model or specialized models are best (building coding agents requires multiple LLM calls; one vs. multiple models is a secret sauce), and distinguishes 'era of experience' from simulation: gaming allows envisioning scenarios and rollouts, while real-world applications have imperfect rollouts requiring actual experience and data collection.
